title: Project exit interview
subtitle: Capture what was done, and why
sequenceRules: @data expands to X7 when the project type is "none of these" or nothing is picked. Otherwise it expands to every question of the data-science module, then every question of the module for each picked type, in the order the types were picked. In the short route, keep only questions with essential=true.

core.text: Tell the story of the project in a couple of minutes.
core.hint: Why it started, what you did, and where it ended up.
prompts: What was the situation at the start?
What did you set out to do?
What did you actually end up doing?
Where did it end up?
core.note: Don't interrupt this answer. The later questions fill in the detail.

core.text: What was the need, and why did this project exist?
prompts: Who needed something, and what was the problem?
What did success look like?
Why this, and why then? What else could the time have gone on?
What did people do about it before, and what was wrong with that?

core.text: What did you do, in order?
prompts: What was the first thing you did, and what came next?
Roughly when was each step?
Did the plan change along the way? Why?
Who was involved, by role?
What works, and how well? Give numbers if you can.
Compared with what: a baseline, the way it was done before?
On which data, and which version of it?
What are you most and least confident about in the results?

core.text: What didn't work, and why did you stop?
prompts: What did you try that failed or went nowhere?
Was it the idea, the data, the tools, the time, or a decision?
What would you not try again? What would you try again with more time?
core.note: People skip this question most often, and it saves the next person the most time.

core.text: What were the main decisions, and why were they made?
prompts: For each: what was decided, and what were the alternatives?
Why this one? What was it about the situation that made it right?
Who decided, by role? When?
Does it still hold, or would you decide differently now?

core.text: What data did you use, and why those sources?
prompts: What was available, and what did you leave out? Why?
Who owns each source, and how did you get access?
What was wrong with the data, and what did you do about it?
core.note: For a data science project, the data science module goes deeper on this. If you use the module, use its data questions instead of this one.

core.text: What state is it in now, and why is it ending or changing hands?
prompts: Is it an idea, a prototype, tested on real data, or in use? Does it work today?
Who uses it, and what do they use it for?
Why is the work ending or moving on, in terms of the work: goal reached, priorities changed, blocked on something?

core.text: What is still open or unfinished?
prompts: What questions are unanswered?
What would you do next, and in what order?
What is blocking it, if anything?

core.text: Where is everything, and how do I run it?
prompts: Where are the code, notebooks, data, models and results?
Can someone rerun it? What do they need: access, an environment, compute, particular versions?
What breaks first?
Is anything missing, or only on someone's own laptop?

core.text: What context would someone not find in the code?
prompts: What domain knowledge does it rely on?
What constraints shaped it?
Which other systems or teams does it depend on?
Which terms would a newcomer not know?
Who knows more, by role?

core.text: If you handed this over in 30 minutes, what would you say?
prompts: What should they read or look at first? What can they ignore?
What will trip them up?
What would you tell them about this that nobody has written down?

questions.text: What data sources did you use, and why did you choose them?
prompts: What was available, and what did you consider but leave out? Why?
Who owns each source, and how did you get access?
Which period, how much data, how often sampled? (Sensor tags, tables, files.)
Was the choice yours, the business's, or simply what you could get?
Is any of it hard to get again, or going to change?

questions.text: What was wrong with the data, and what did you do about it?
prompts: Gaps, wrong units, drift, faulty sensors, duplicates, missing labels?
Was context missing, such as design information, operating mode or maintenance records?
Did changes to sensors or assets reach you late, or not at all?
How did you handle each problem, and who could fix it at the source?

questions.text: How did you prepare the data?
prompts: Cleaning, aggregating, filling gaps, building features.
What assumptions are built into those steps?
Could someone reuse the preparation code on a new project?

questions.text: How did you judge whether it worked?
prompts: Which measure did you use, and who agreed it was the right one?
What was the baseline: the current method, or something simple?
How did you validate: on which data, and was it separate from what you built on?
What was the result in numbers, and what would have counted as good enough?

questions.text: What domain knowledge did you need, and who gave it to you?
prompts: Which engineers or experts shaped the approach?
Was there something they told you that changed what you did?
What would you ask them earlier next time?

questions.text: How close is it to being used for real?
prompts: Where is it: an idea, a prototype, tested on real data, or in use?
Who would use it, and what decision would it help with?
What would have to be true to run it every day: live data, an owner, support, approvals?

questions.text: Could someone else rerun it?
prompts: What do they need: data access, an environment, compute, specific versions?
Where are the notebooks, pipelines and results?
What breaks first?

questions.text: What counts as an anomaly here, and who decided?
prompts: What does a real event look like: an equipment fault, a process upset, a sensor fault?
Is a bad sensor an anomaly, or a data problem?
What should happen when one is found?

questions.text: What labelled examples did you have, and did you check against past events?
prompts: How many examples, from where (incident logs, maintenance records, engineers' judgement)?
How reliable are the labels? Were real events left unlabelled?
Did you test the method on known past incidents? What did it catch, miss, or give early warning of?

questions.text: What approaches did you try, and how did they compare?
prompts: Fixed limits or rules, statistical methods, machine learning, learning from normal data only?
Why did you keep or drop each?

questions.text: How did you deal with false alarms and missed events?
prompts: What false alarm rate could users tolerate?
What trade-off did you choose, and who agreed it?
How did engineers or operators react to the alerts?

questions.text: How did you tell bad data from a real anomaly?
prompts: Frozen values, gaps, spikes, interpolation?
Where in the pipeline is that decided?

questions.text: How did you handle changes in what is normal?
prompts: Operating modes, seasons, maintenance, equipment changes, drift?
How often does it need retraining or resetting?

questions.text: What was forecast, and what decision does it feed?
prompts: Which quantity, how far ahead (the horizon), and how often (the time resolution)?
Who uses the forecast, and for what?

questions.text: What was the baseline, and how did the model compare?
prompts: A naive or seasonal forecast, or the forecast already in use?
By how much did you beat it, or fail to, and on which measure?

questions.text: What drives the series?
prompts: Seasonality, trends, outside drivers such as weather, plans, prices or operating conditions?
Which extra data did you add, and why?

questions.text: How did you validate?
prompts: Backtests that respect time order? Which horizons did you test?
How far back did you train, and how often would it be retrained?

questions.text: Where does it fail?
prompts: Regime changes, outliers, gaps, extreme values, long horizons?
Do users need a range, not just one number?

questions.text: How many series, and how did you handle scale?
prompts: One model per series or a shared one?
What about a new series with no history?

questions.text: What is being scheduled, and what makes a schedule good?
prompts: What is the objective: cost, delay, utilisation, risk, safety?
Who agreed it? Do the aims conflict?

questions.text: Which constraints did you include, and which did you leave out?
prompts: Resources, order of tasks, availability, time windows, rules and regulations?
Why were some left out?

questions.text: Where did the inputs come from, and how reliable are they?
prompts: Durations, availability, demand.
How far apart are estimates and actuals?

questions.text: What approach did you use, and why?
prompts: Rules of thumb, mathematical optimisation with a solver, search heuristics, simulation, machine learning?
How large a problem could it handle, and how long did it take to run?

questions.text: How did it compare with how scheduling is done today?
prompts: A manual plan, or an existing tool?
How did you measure the difference, for example by replaying past periods?
What can it not do yet?

questions.text: What do the schedulers know that the model doesn't?
prompts: Unwritten rules and exceptions.
How do they handle disruptions and re-planning?
Did they trust the output?

questions.text: What are the classes, who defined them, and how clear are the boundaries?
prompts: Could two experts disagree about which class something belongs to?

questions.text: Where did the labels come from?
prompts: How many per class, who labelled them, how reliable?
Is one class much rarer than the others?

questions.text: Which inputs mattered, and which methods did you try?
prompts: Why did you keep or drop each?

questions.text: How did you measure it, and which mistakes matter most?
prompts: Missing a case or flagging a wrong one: which costs more?
Which classes get confused?
How does it compare with the baseline or with a person doing the same job?

questions.text: How did you check it works on new data?
prompts: Did you split by time, by asset or by site?
Any risk that information leaked from the answer into the inputs?
Have you seen drift?

questions.text: What happens when it is unsure or wrong?
prompts: Is there a confidence threshold or a human check?
What does a wrong call cost?

questions.text: What is being recognised, and what do the images look like?
prompts: Which classes, who defined them, and how clear are the boundaries?
Where do the images come from: which cameras or sources, what resolution, what angles and lighting?
Is it single images or video?

questions.text: Where did the images and labels come from?
prompts: How many images, and how many per class? Are some classes rare?
Who labelled them, with what instructions, and how often did labellers disagree?
How were hard or ambiguous cases handled?

questions.text: What approach did you use, and why?
prompts: A ready-made model used as it is, a pretrained model adapted to your images, or one trained from scratch?
Anything you did to make the images more varied or the data cleaner?
Why did you keep or drop each option?

questions.text: How did you measure it, and which mistakes matter most?
prompts: Missing a case or flagging a wrong one: which costs more?
Which classes get confused, and why do you think so?
How does it compare with a person doing the same job?

questions.text: How did you check it on new conditions?
prompts: Different cameras, sites, lighting, weather or time of day?
Did frames from the same video end up on both sides of the split, making results look better than they are?
What happened when conditions changed?

questions.text: What happens when it is unsure or wrong?
prompts: Is there a confidence threshold or a human check?
What does a wrong call cost?

questions.text: Where would it run, and how fast must it be?
prompts: On a camera or device, on a nearby computer, or in the cloud?
How many images a second, and how quickly must the answer arrive?
Who looks at the results, and what happens to the stored images?

questions.text: How would you describe the problem in one sentence to someone outside the team?
What kind of method did you use, and why that one?
What did you compare it against?
prompts: A baseline, or current practice.

questions.text: What did you measure, and what was the result?
What would you tell someone choosing a method for a similar problem?
